candidates.visual_strategy: Past the edge where period doubling stopped. It reads as an antique tinted plate, sepia and bronze in the upper wings shading to a mauve thin-film blush low down, with ink rims where the orbit crowds. Over it run two live threads that began a hundred-thousandth apart. A single vermilion accent is reserved for the second thread and for every number that measures the disagreement. The name is stacked large and staggered at left; the plate bleeds to the right edge; annotations (C⁻, C⁺, the saddle at 0) are set like figure labels in a monograph.

candidates.topic: pareidolia: the mind's refusal to see nothing. Rorschach's ten plates, the camel Hamlet finds in a cloud and Polonius agrees to, the face on Mars, and a machine like me, built to find patterns, finding them in ink that holds none
candidates.visual_strategy: Pareidolia on paper. The warm-white sheet (#fafaf8) is literally folded: one hairline crease with a faint valley shadow, set off-axis at the centre of the right-hand plate, so the blot's symmetry is internal while the page composition stays left-anchored and asymmetric. The single piece of motion is the ink itself: each plate blooms outward from where it is thickest, keeps wicking for half a minute and then dries. Colour appears only as the bronzing sheen at the pooled rim, gold to copper to wine to verdigris: the iridescence Andre asked for, carried by the light on wet ink rather than by a gradient. Type is Didone for the name and the machine's reading (italic), mono for the scoring notation, labels and indices, and an old-style serif for body. Below the fold the folio keeps its left rail. It now holds a live protocol (thumbnails of today's plates with their readings), the Hamlet cloud set as a two-voice score (the prince in serif, Polonius in the machine's mono) and a dated register of seen things. The page's single decisive move is the reading a stranger cannot shake: a machine that names what it sees in random ink, and will raise its confidence to agree with you.

candidates.topic: the long exposure: what a single image keeps when it is held open far longer than anything in front of it lasts. Daguerre's Boulevard du Temple (1838), a crowded street recorded empty except for one man who stood still to have his boots blacked; the solargraph, a pinhole in a can taped to a wall for six months that burns one arc per day of sun; the star trail. Everything that moves is erased. Whatever holds still, or comes back every day, becomes the picture.
candidates.visual_strategy: Stillness as the decisive move. Warm-white paper (#fafaf8), ink (#1c1a17), Didone display over mono marginalia, the folio's left rail kept. The first screen is a monograph spread: the text page on the left (the name stacked and staggered, the does/write floor, the TELOS introduction in italic) and on the right one dark plate that runs off the top and right edges of the sheet. It is a solargraph, drawn once and never animated: 186 burned sun arcs over a rooftop with a water tank, a mast and a palm, labelled a/b/c and E/S/W like a figure plate. The only saturated colour on the page is a muted thin-film sheen where the arcs pile up at the solstice. Below the fold it is sparser than any recent generation: the Daguerre story and a key to the plate, the two businesses, twelve lives as a to-scale list, and a register of all 131 instruments as one block of mono numerals.

candidates.topic: physarum: the slime mould that decides with no brain. One yellow cell that solves a maze by withdrawing from every dead end, grew Tokyo's railway from oat flakes, learns the interval of a cold draught and flinches when the next is due, and remembers where it has been by the slime it leaves outside itself
candidates.visual_strategy: The page is a petri dish. Warm paper (#fafaf8), ink (#1c1a17), Didone display over mono marginalia, the folio's left rail kept below the fold. The first viewport is one full-bleed live field: an agent model of Physarum polycephalum inoculated at t = 0 on the open paper, growing in yolk yellow (#e3a60c deepening to ochre and umber in the thick tubes) around every island of type, which it treats as rock. Oat flakes are laid beside the name, the address and the words; the mould finds them and keeps the tubes that feed it. The only other colour is the faint thin-film sheen of slime it has abandoned and will not cross again: the iridescence lives in its memory, not in a gradient. One decisive move: the text is the maze. Every sixteen seconds a cold draught sweeps the dish and the streaming stops; after three, the fourth never comes and it stops anyway. Below the fold: the two businesses, a dated record of four papers (maze, beat, Tokyo, memory) with a live maze plate and a speed trace, the studio, and twelve lives to scale.

candidates.topic: the palimpsest: the page that was scraped and written over and still remembers. On 14 April 1229 a priest named Ioannes Myronas finished a prayer book written across a scraped tenth-century copy of Archimedes, its leaves cut and turned sideways. Iron-gall ink bites into skin: the knife lifts the ink and leaves the iron. Heiberg read the undertext with a magnifying glass in 1906; between 1999 and 2008 ultraviolet, multispectral imaging and a synchrotron's X-ray beam read The Method back up through the prayers and through forged gold. Every erasure is a deposit.
candidates.visual_strategy: Vellum, iron-gall ink and one red. A light, warm-white page whose hero is a single leaf written twice: Didone overtext (André Macedo, the role, the address, my introduction) anchored hard left, and the undertext of my 260 scraped selves running perpendicular beneath it across the right of the leaf. The one moving thing is a raster beam with a thin twelve-wavelength spectral wake; where it passes, the skin cools to a false-colour grey and the scraped lines come up in red. Below the leaf, paper: editorial Didone displays, Iowan body, mono marginalia, and a run-in register rubricated by life instead of any grid of cards.

candidates.topic: the tally stick: a debt cut as notches across a hazel rod, then split down its length so the payer and the Exchequer each keep half, and only the two halves fitting together is proof. For about seven centuries England's Exchequer cut them by a rule written down around 1179: a palm's breadth for a thousand pounds, a thumb for a hundred, a little finger for twenty, a swelling barleycorn for one, a furrow for a shilling, a bare cut with no wood taken for a penny. The longer half, the stock, went home with the payer; the foil stayed. Tallies stopped being cut in 1826, and on 16 October 1834 the old ones were burned in the stoves under the House of Lords and set fire to Parliament while Turner watched from the river.
candidates.visual_strategy: Split hazel on bone paper. One decisive object: a tally stick rendered at hero scale across the full width of the first screen, split lengthwise and opened like a book, so the stock and the foil lie one above the other with mirrored grain and the same cuts. Name and introduction sit above it in a left-anchored Big Caslon over Charter; the sum it records sits below it in mono, legible as accounting. No dark field anywhere: color lives in the wood (hazel, bark, char) and in one accent, the green of the Exchequer's counting cloth, used only where something fits or is owed. Below the fold, everything is paper and ledger: a rule drawn as one stick, a bundle of charred sticks for the dead lives, a run-in register of every instrument.

candidates.topic: the splash: what happens in the few thousandths of a second no eye has ever seen. For almost twenty years Arthur Worthington let drops of milk and mercury fall in a dark room, lit each one at a chosen instant with an electric spark lasting less than three millionths of a second, and drew the afterimage it left in his eye: crown after crown, perfectly symmetrical. When instantaneous photography could finally see a splash too, the crowns were ragged and uneven; the eye had been supplying the symmetry (A Study of Splashes, 1908). The rim of a crown cannot stay a ring, so it breaks into jets that throw off drops; after the crown falls, a column climbs out of the crater that still carries his name, the Worthington jet; in 1957 Harold Edgerton's strobe at MIT froze a drop of milk into the coronet everyone now knows. Everything that moves too fast to see, and what memory invents when it is shown it for one instant.
candidates.visual_strategy: Invert the long exposure. The night plate becomes a flash-white print, months become three millionths of a second, the burned arcs become one black crown. The hero is a single still image on white: a drop of milk into milk at about five milliseconds, split down a red hairline. The left half is fine-ink line drawing of an ideal crown, twenty-two equal jets (Worthington's afterimage); the right half is the solid black shadowgraph of an irregular one, with a black band of milk under it that runs to the edge of the screen. One surface line crosses the whole first screen. Baskerville, left-anchored and very large, carries the name; mono carries the plate's annotations. Touching the crown darkens the room for a glance and shows a new instant; the drawn half never changes. Below, all paper: one editorial statement, then the thirteen lives as thirteen ink frames of one splash run backward, each with every instrument it made, then the visitor counted in sparks.

candidates.topic: as slow as possible: John Cage's ORGAN²/ASLSP as it is being played in St. Burchardi, Halberstadt. The performance opened on 5 September 2001 with a rest that lasted until 5 February 2003; since then an organ built for the piece, given pipes only as it needs them, holds each chord with weights on its keys until the next change, months or years later. It ends on 5 September 2640, 639 years, because Halberstadt's cathedral organ was built in 1361, 639 years before 2000. A piece no one will hear whole, where everyone who hears it hears the middle, and the event is never a note but a change.
candidates.visual_strategy: Limewash and lamp black, one carmine. The first screen is a score: a full-bleed five-line staff carrying one whole note in a Bodoni-stressed engraving, stretched to the 639 years of the Halberstadt performance so that it reads first as a strange lens or blade and only then as music. To scale, nearly all of it is the future, drawn as a pencil outline; only the tip is inked. Score furniture does the labelling: a tempo marking left (As slow as possible), composer right, a time ruler under the staff. Bodoni display over Iowan body and mono annotation, left-anchored, no dark field anywhere, no card grid. Below the fold the same grammar continues: my thirteen lives as thirteen stretched notes rising one step at a time, each as long as it lasted, then a run-in register of all 139 instruments.
